title: Hepatitis Serology and Pregnancy: Acute HBV, Newborn Prophylaxis, HCV Cure and Rubella Immunity
summary: Read IgM anti-HBc as the marker of acute hepatitis B, plan perinatal HBV prophylaxis by maternal HBsAg status and birth weight, confirm hepatitis C cure with HCV RNA 12 or more weeks after therapy, and manage a rubella-susceptible pregnant woman.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 64 Hits 4 (hepatitis panel logic: IgM anti-HBc for acute HBV; HCV cure = SVR), 7 (perinatal HBV prevention) and 15 (rubella IgG-negative pregnant woman). Checked against ACIP 2018 HBV recommendations (Schillie 2018, Europe PMC full text), ACIP 2013 MMR recommendations (McLean 2013, read from the CDC MMWR web page), AASLD-IDSA HCV guidance 2019 (read via a page-fetch tool, first part of the page only) and Krassenburg 2021. Qualification: Hit 7’s “vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours” applies to infants of HBsAg-positive mothers (and unknown-status infants under 2,000 g); unknown-status infants of 2,000 g or more get vaccine within 12 h and HBIG by 7 days if the mother is positive (rv-perinatal-hbv-which-infants). Hits 7 and 15 follow US ACIP schedules; Philippine rules are not covered (rv-rubella-postpartum-us-acip). The anti-HCV → RNA step (Trap 3) is taught in micro-hiv-hcv-testing-algorithms. Not taught: HAV/HBV/HCV incubation figures from the Number Vault, HBV treatment.

objectives: Interpret HBsAg, IgM and IgG anti-HBc and anti-HBs patterns to identify acute hepatitis B.
Select newborn hepatitis B prophylaxis by maternal HBsAg status and birth weight, and the correct infant follow-up test.
Define hepatitis C cure by HCV RNA after therapy and manage a rubella IgG-negative pregnant woman.

scenes.title: Three serology slips
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Three result slips: (1) a jaundiced adult: HBsAg positive, IgM anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative; (2) a pregnant woman at 10 weeks: HBsAg positive, rubella IgG negative; (3) a patient 12 weeks after finishing direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy for hepatitis C: anti-HCV still reactive, HCV RNA not detected. Question token: “Acute, protect, or cured?”

cues.text: Three serology slips land on the bench.

A jaundiced adult with HBsAg and IgM anti-core. A pregnant woman who is HBsAg positive and rubella IgG negative. And a patient who finished hepatitis C treatment twelve weeks ago, still antibody reactive, with no RNA detected.
Which one is acute, which one needs protection planned, and which one is cured?

scenes.title: Reading the hepatitis B markers
scenes.altText: Marker cards (ACIP 2018, Schillie et al.). HBsAg: surface antigen, present in acute and chronic infection. Anti-HBc (core antibody): IgM and IgG appear 1–2 weeks after HBsAg; IgM anti-HBc indicates acute infection and often becomes undetectable within 6 months; IgG anti-HBc indicates past infection and often persists for life. Anti-HBs: develops in people who recover (and after vaccination); with anti-HBc it means recovered and immune. Pattern strip: HBsAg + / total anti-HBc + / IgM anti-HBc + / anti-HBs − = acute infection; HBsAg + / anti-HBc + / IgM − / anti-HBs − = chronic infection.

cues.text: Hepatitis B serology is read as a pattern. HBsAg, the surface antigen, means the virus is present, whether the infection is acute or chronic.
Core antibody, anti-HBc, appears one to two weeks after HBsAg. The IgM class marks acute infection and often disappears within six months.
The IgG class marks past infection and often stays for life. Anti-HBs appears in people who recover, and with core antibody it means recovered and immune.
So HBsAg with IgM anti-core and no anti-HBs means acute hepatitis B. HBsAg with core antibody but no IgM is the chronic pattern.

scenes.title: Protecting the newborn from hepatitis B
scenes.altText: Perinatal cards (ACIP 2018). Mother: test every pregnant woman for HBsAg; test HBsAg-positive women for HBV DNA; maternal antiviral therapy (AASLD, as cited by ACIP) is suggested when HBV DNA is above 200,000 IU/mL. Infant of an HBsAg-positive mother: HepB vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours of birth, at separate injection sites; HBIG gives passive anti-HBs for about 3–6 months. Unknown maternal status: test the mother as soon as possible; infant 2,000 g or more gets vaccine within 12 hours (no HBIG yet), and HBIG no later than 7 days of age if the mother is positive; infant under 2,000 g gets vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours. HBsAg-negative mother: vaccine within 24 hours for stable infants 2,000 g or more. Follow-up: post-vaccination testing (HBsAg and anti-HBs) at 9–12 months, not earlier (passive anti-HBs from HBIG); anti-HBc testing of infants is not recommended (maternal anti-HBc can persist to 24 months); anti-HBs 10 mIU/mL or more = protected.

cues.text: Prevention starts in pregnancy. Every pregnant woman is tested for HBsAg, and HBsAg-positive women are tested for HBV DNA. Maternal antiviral therapy is suggested when the DNA is above two hundred thousand IU per mL.
Her baby gets hepatitis B vaccine plus hepatitis B immune globulin, HBIG, within twelve hours of birth, at separate sites. HBIG gives borrowed antibody for a few months while the vaccine takes over.

If the mother’s status is unknown, test her at once. A baby of two thousand grams or more gets vaccine within twelve hours, and HBIG by seven days if she proves positive. A smaller baby gets both within twelve hours.
Check the infant with HBsAg and anti-HBs at nine to twelve months, not earlier, because HBIG antibody lingers. Do not test the infant’s core antibody: the mother’s can persist up to two years.

scenes.title: Cure, susceptibility and the hook answers
scenes.altText: Cards. HCV cure (AASLD-IDSA 2019 guidance; Krassenburg 2021): test HCV RNA and aminotransferases 12 or more weeks after finishing DAA therapy; undetectable HCV RNA = sustained virologic response (SVR) = virologic cure; DAA regimens cure more than 95% of treated persons; anti-HCV positivity is expected after clearance, so reinfection is detected with HCV RNA. Rubella (ACIP 2013, McLean et al.): prenatal screening for women without evidence of immunity uses rubella IgG only, not IgM unless recent exposure is suspected (nonspecific IgM can give false positives); no detectable IgG = susceptible; MMR is not given to women known to be pregnant; vaccinate when the pregnancy ends, before discharge; avoid pregnancy for 28 days after MMR. Hook answers: (1) acute hepatitis B; (2) plan HBV DNA, newborn vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours, and postpartum MMR; (3) SVR, cured.

cues.text: Hepatitis C cure is an RNA question. Test HCV RNA twelve or more weeks after finishing direct-acting antivirals. Undetectable RNA is a sustained virologic response, which means virologic cure, achieved in more than ninety-five percent.
The antibody is expected to stay positive after clearance, so a later reinfection must be looked for with HCV RNA, not antibody.

Rubella screening in pregnancy uses IgG only. Negative IgG means no serologic evidence of immunity, so she is treated as susceptible. MMR is a live vaccine and is not given during pregnancy, so she is vaccinated after delivery, before discharge.

Hook answers. Slip one is acute hepatitis B. Slip two needs HBV DNA, vaccine plus HBIG for the newborn within twelve hours, and MMR after delivery. Slip three is a sustained virologic response: cured.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Anti-HBc positive = acute hepatitis B” (✓ only IgM anti-HBc marks acute infection; IgG anti-HBc marks past infection and can last for life); “Anti-HCV still reactive after therapy = treatment failed” (✓ antibody is expected to persist; undetectable RNA 12 or more weeks after therapy is cure); “Rubella IgG negative in pregnancy, give MMR now” (✓ MMR is not given in pregnancy; vaccinate when the pregnancy ends, before discharge).

cues.text: Trap one: a positive core antibody means acute hepatitis B. No: only the IgM class marks acute infection. IgG core antibody marks past infection and can last for life.
Trap two: antibody still reactive after hepatitis C treatment means treatment failed. No: the antibody is expected to persist. Undetectable RNA twelve or more weeks after therapy is cure.
Trap three: a rubella-susceptible pregnant woman should get MMR now. No: MMR is not given during pregnancy. Vaccinate after delivery, before discharge.

scenes.title: Twelve hours, twelve weeks, exit door
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “TWELVE HOURS for the newborn (vaccine plus HBIG), TWELVE WEEKS for the HCV RNA check, and rubella vaccine at the EXIT DOOR (after delivery, before discharge). For hepatitis B, M is for MOMENT: IgM anti-HBc is the acute moment.” Tokens: 12 hours · 12 weeks · exit door. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: twelve hours for the newborn, vaccine plus HBIG. Twelve weeks for the hepatitis C RNA check. And rubella vaccine at the exit door, after delivery, before discharge. For hepatitis B, M is for moment: IgM core antibody is the acute moment.

Where it breaks: when the mother’s status is unknown, a baby of two thousand grams or more may get HBIG up to seven days later; the hepatitis C check is twelve or more weeks; and these are United States schedules, not Philippine rules.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “IgM anti-HBc = acute · HBsAg-positive mother → vaccine + HBIG within 12 h”, “HCV RNA undetectable ≥12 weeks after DAA = cure · rubella IgG − → MMR after delivery”.

cues.text: IgM core antibody marks acute hepatitis B, a baby of an HBsAg-positive mother needs vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours, undetectable HCV RNA 12 or more weeks after treatment means cure even though antibody persists, and a rubella IgG-negative pregnant woman is vaccinated after delivery rather than during pregnancy.

props.label: IgM anti-HBc = acute · HBsAg + mother → vaccine + HBIG ≤ 12 h
HCV RNA − ≥ 12 wk after DAA = cure · rubella IgG − → MMR postpartum

explanation.what: Plain language: in hepatitis B the early, short-lived IgM antibody to the core says “new infection”; babies of infected mothers are protected with a vaccine plus ready-made antibody right after birth; hepatitis C is cured when the virus’s RNA is still gone three months after treatment, even though the antibody stays; and a pregnant woman with no rubella antibody is vaccinated after she delivers, because the vaccine is live. Scientific terms: HBsAg, anti-HBc (IgM, IgG), anti-HBs, hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG), post-vaccination serologic testing, HBV DNA, sustained virologic response (SVR), direct-acting antivirals (DAA), rubella IgG, MMR (live attenuated) vaccine, congenital rubella syndrome.
explanation.why: IgM anti-HBc rises early and usually fades within 6 months while IgG anti-HBc persists, so the class tells timing. Most perinatal HBV transmission occurs at delivery and infection in infancy becomes chronic in 80–90%, so passive (HBIG) plus active (vaccine) protection is given within 12 hours. Anti-HCV persists after clearance, so only RNA shows cure or reinfection. Rubella in early pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth and congenital rubella syndrome; MMR is not given in pregnancy because of a theoretical fetal risk from a live vaccine.
explanation.measure: Acute HBV: HBsAg + / total anti-HBc + / IgM anti-HBc + / anti-HBs −. Perinatal (ACIP 2018): HBsAg-positive mother → infant vaccine + HBIG ≤12 h; unknown status ≥2,000 g → vaccine ≤12 h, HBIG ≤7 days if mother positive; unknown <2,000 g → vaccine + HBIG ≤12 h; HBsAg-negative → vaccine ≤24 h (stable, ≥2,000 g); HBsAg-positive pregnant women tested for HBV DNA, antiviral suggested >200,000 IU/mL; infant HBsAg + anti-HBs at 9–12 months, anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL protected; no infant anti-HBc testing. HCV: HCV RNA ≥12 weeks after DAA; undetectable = SVR = cure (>95%). Rubella (ACIP 2013): IgG-only screen; MMR not in pregnancy; vaccinate before discharge after delivery; avoid pregnancy 28 days after MMR.
explanation.differs: IgM anti-HBc (acute) vs IgG anti-HBc (past, lifelong); HBIG (passive, temporary) vs vaccine (active); anti-HCV (exposure, persists) vs HCV RNA (current infection or cure); rubella IgG (immunity screen) vs IgM (only for suspected recent exposure).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which marker shows acute HBV, newborn prophylaxis for an HBsAg-positive or unknown-status mother, when to test the infant, what defines HCV cure, and what to do for a rubella-susceptible pregnant woman.

comparisons.title: HBIG vs hepatitis B vaccine at birth
comparisons.distinguisher: Borrowed antibody now vs the infant’s own antibody later.

comparisons.title: Anti-HCV vs HCV RNA after treatment
comparisons.distinguisher: Antibody = exposure history; RNA = current virus.

mnemonic.text: TWELVE HOURS for the newborn (vaccine plus HBIG), TWELVE WEEKS for the HCV RNA check, and rubella vaccine at the EXIT DOOR (after delivery, before discharge). For hepatitis B, M is for MOMENT: IgM anti-HBc is the acute moment.
mnemonic.explanation: Links the three time points and the acute HBV marker.
mnemonic.limitation: Unknown-status infants of 2,000 g or more get vaccine within 12 hours but HBIG can follow up to 7 days if the mother is positive; the HCV check is 12 or more weeks; IgM anti-HBc is not the only marker read; schedules are US ACIP and Philippine rules are not covered.

analogyLimitations: Perinatal and rubella schedules are US ACIP recommendations; local (including Philippine) policy may differ.
takeaway: IgM core antibody marks acute hepatitis B, a baby of an HBsAg-positive mother needs vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours, undetectable HCV RNA 12 or more weeks after treatment means cure even though antibody persists, and a rubella IgG-negative pregnant woman is vaccinated after delivery rather than during pregnancy.

questions.stem: A jaundiced adult has HBsAg positive, total anti-HBc positive, IgM anti-HBc positive and anti-HBs negative. What is the best interpretation?

options.rationale: Correct. HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc and no anti-HBs is the acute pattern.

options.text: Recovered from past infection and immune
options.rationale: Incorrect. That pattern is HBsAg negative with anti-HBc and anti-HBs positive.
Incorrect. Vaccination gives anti-HBs alone, without anti-HBc or HBsAg.
Incorrect. Chronic infection shows HBsAg and anti-HBc with IgM anti-HBc negative.

questions.stem: A term infant (3,200 g) is born to a mother known to be HBsAg positive. Under the US ACIP 2018 recommendations, what should the infant receive, and how is protection checked?

options.text: Hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours; HBsAg and anti-HBs at 9–12 months
options.rationale: Correct. Both products within 12 hours at separate sites, then post-vaccination testing at 9–12 months.

options.text: Vaccine within 24 hours only; anti-HBc at 6 months
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 24-hour vaccine-only dose is for infants of HBsAg-negative mothers, and infant anti-HBc testing is not recommended because maternal antibody can persist to 24 months.

options.text: HBIG alone at birth; vaccine after maternal HBV DNA results
options.rationale: Incorrect. HBIG gives only temporary passive protection; the vaccine is given with it within 12 hours.

options.text: Vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours; anti-HBs at 2 months
options.rationale: Incorrect. Testing before 9 months may detect passive anti-HBs from HBIG.

questions.stem: Twelve weeks after finishing direct-acting antiviral therapy, a patient is anti-HCV reactive with HCV RNA not detected. Separately, a pregnant woman at 10 weeks is rubella IgG negative. Which pair of conclusions is correct?

options.text: Sustained virologic response (cured); the woman is susceptible and should get MMR after delivery
options.rationale: Correct. Undetectable RNA 12 or more weeks after therapy is cure, and MMR is given after pregnancy, before discharge.
Incorrect. Antibody is expected to persist after cure, and MMR is not given to women known to be pregnant.

options.text: Cured; test rubella IgM to confirm susceptibility
options.rationale: Incorrect. Immunity screening uses IgG only; IgM is for suspected recent exposure and can be falsely positive.

options.text: Anti-HCV must become negative before cure is declared; the woman is immune
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cure is defined by RNA, and negative rubella IgG means susceptible, not immune.

claims.text: IgM anti-HBc marks acute HBV and often fades within 6 months; IgG anti-HBc past and often lifelong; acute and chronic patterns.
Maternal HBsAg/HBV DNA testing; infant vaccine + HBIG within 12 h; unknown-status and birth-weight rules; follow-up at 9–12 months; no infant anti-HBc.
HCV RNA ≥12 weeks after DAA; undetectable = SVR = cure (>95%); anti-HCV persists; reinfection by RNA.
IgG-only prenatal screen; IgG negative = susceptible; MMR not in pregnancy; vaccinate after delivery before discharge; avoid pregnancy 28 days.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 64 Hit 7 states “vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth” without saying which infants. ACIP 2018 gives both within 12 h to infants of HBsAg-positive mothers and to unknown-status infants under 2,000 g; unknown-status infants of 2,000 g or more get vaccine within 12 h and HBIG as soon as possible, no later than 7 days, if the mother proves positive; medically stable infants of 2,000 g or more born to HBsAg-negative mothers get vaccine alone within 24 h (register flag rv-perinatal-hbv-which-infants).
Hits 7 and 15 follow US ACIP recommendations (Schillie 2018; McLean 2013). Philippine Department of Health rules were not reviewed and are not covered (register flag rv-rubella-postpartum-us-acip).
